- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates drop; adjust downward by 2–5% relative to recent low.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days post-spike.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and price is volatile, model often fails to capture mean reversion; add a “reversion buffer” to forecast: if price deviates >3σ from 30-day mean, pull back toward mean.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but sentiment is neutral or bearish, reduce forecast slope; avoid “trend-following” bias in low-sentiment periods.
- In high-sentiment periods, model often ignores volatility; add volatility-adjusted buffer: if sentiment >0.7, forecast should include 1–2% downward risk premium unless confirmed breakout.
